# Cypher

[[neo4j]]'s declarative query language. Patterns are written as ASCII-art graphs —
`(a)-[:REL]->(b)` — which makes a traversal query look like the thing it traverses.

## What lab 6 uses it for

Two `.cypher` scripts in [[discrete-mathematics-laboratories]] carrying the whole deliverable:

**Constraints first.** Node-key uniqueness constraints created before any data lands, so `MERGE` is
index-backed rather than a full scan.

**`LOAD CSV` + `MERGE` import.** `LOAD CSV WITH HEADERS` streams the source file from the Desktop
import folder; `MERGE` matches-or-creates so re-running the script is a no-op rather than a
duplication. One `:Object` per row, 39 objects and 975 `HAS_VALUE` relationships. This is the graph
half of [[idempotent-loading]].

The distinction that matters and is easy to get wrong: **`CREATE` always creates, `MERGE` matches the
whole pattern or creates the whole pattern.** `MERGE` on a pattern with an unmatched middle node
creates the entire path, so the safe idiom is to `MERGE` nodes separately, then `MERGE` the
relationship between them — which is what the script does.

**Q0–Q6 report queries** reading the [[pawlak-information-system]] back out: counts, per-attribute
value distributions, and the grade/class grouping traversals.

## Read beside its analogue

`lab6_Neo4j/viewer/pawlak.js` reimplements each of these queries in plain JavaScript and renders the
result **next to the Cypher that produces it**. Reading a graph query beside the imperative loop it
replaces is the most direct way to see what the declarative form is buying — see
[[dual-implementation-as-cross-check]].

## Note

`guide.txt` explicitly steers away from Neo4j's GUI import tool toward scripts —
[[cypher-scripts-over-neo4j-import-tool]] — which is what makes the import reproducible at all.
